title: Photo-induced reduction of CO2 to CO with hydrogen over plasmonic Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs core/shell hetero-junction under UV and visible light
abstract:
Ag-NPs-promoted TiO2 nanowires (TiO2 NWs) core/shell hetero-junction with plasmonic properties for selective CO production in photo-induced CO2-hydrogen system has been investigated. Ag-NPs were photo-deposited over the TiO2 NWs and characterized by XRD, TEM, N2-adsorption-desorption, XPS, UV–vis and PL spectroscopy. Ag-NPs in metal-state were successfully coated on the TiO2 NWs surface, producing core-shell hetero-junction. Ag-NPs coated over TiO2 NWs exhibited strong absorption of visible light due to localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) excitation, trapped electrons and hindered charges recombination rate. The synergistic effect of Ag-NPs coated over TiO2 NWs for CO2 conversion was evaluated in a gas-phase system under UV and visible light irradiation. The plasmonic Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs demonstrated excellent photoactivity in the reduction of CO2 into CO, CH4 and CH3OH under visible light irradiation. The results show that 3wt.% Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs was found to be the most active, giving the highest CO evolution of 983μmole-g-catal.−1
                     h−1 at selectivity 98%. This amount of CO produced was 23 times more than the TiO2 NWs and 109 times larger than the yield of CO produced over the pure TiO2. More importantly, the quantum yield was substantially enhanced for CO evolution. The LSPR excitation and synergic effect of Ag-NPs which can effectively accelerate the charge separation was proposed to be responsible for the enhancement of photocatalytic activity. The photo-stability of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs evidenced in cyclic runs for selective CO production under visible light, yet photoactivity declined over the irradiation time under UV-light. The reaction mechanism to describe the reaction pathways is also presented.
paragraphs: The energy shortages and increase of CO2 concentration in the atmosphere due to growing consumption of fossil fuels have invigorated great concerns in the last few decades. Many approaches have been developed for CO2 utilization, yet artificial photosynthesis for photocatalytic reduction of CO2 provides alternative prospective for the storage of solar energy into useful chemicals and fuels. Therefore, conversion of CO2 into useful carbon sources such as CO, CH4, CH3OH HCHO and HCOOH using solar energy is one of the ideal way to address both the global warming and energy shortage problems. However, the yield and selectivity reported are below the acceptable level of commercialization. Efficient photocatalytic CO2 reduction requires semiconductor materials that could meet certain stringent criteria.

In photocatalytic conversion of CO2, TiO2 is one of the well-studied photocatalysts and has been received increasing attentions due to its advantages such as inexpensive, available in excess, nontoxic, photo-stable and strong oxidative potential. However, TiO2 as a photocatalyst has some disadvantages such as the large band gap energy (∼3.20eV for anatase, ∼3.0eV for rutile) which only allows the absorption of ultraviolet (UV) irradiation. Additionally, it has high recombination rate of photo-generated (e−/h+) charges and uncontrolled photoreduction selectivity. To improve its photocatalytic performance, many strategies have been developed such as metals-loading, semiconductors coupling and co-catalysts modifications.

Adding metals to semiconductor to establish metal/semiconductor hetero-junction could enhanced photocatalytic activity under visible light irradiations. Recently, metals such as gold (Au), silver (Ag) and copper (Cu) are considered as promising materials for CO2 reduction applications for the reason that CO weakly binds on their surfaces. Mainly, Cu produced a mixture of hydrocarbons such as CH4, CH3OH, C2H4 and HCOOH, however, Au and Ag demonstrated highly selective for CO2 to CO conversion. Many efforts have been performed in the use of these metals to enhance photocatalytic performance of TiO2. For example, Au-loaded TiO2 nanoparticles were investigated for selective photocatalytic CO2 conversion to CO, production of CH4 in the photocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction using Cu/TiO2 photocatalyst, the use of Pt-Cu2O-TiO2 co-catalysts for the reduction of CO2 to CH4, Cu-loaded In2O3/TiO2 photocatalysts for the conversion of CO2 to CH4 and CH3OH, modification of MWCNT/TiO2 by Ag for enhanced photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2O to CH4 and C2H4 and incorporation of Cu into TiO2 for photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH4.

To date, nanostructured titanium dioxide (TiO2) is of great interest owing to larger surface area with excellent optical and photocatalytic properties, thus offer direct pathways for effectively collecting photons and/or electrons. Many types of nanostructured TiO2 have been investigated such as nanowires, nanosheets, nanorods and nanotubes. However, in the development of visible light responsive TiO2 nanostructures, narrowing the band gap energy of TiO2 will establish a benchmark for the sunlight-driven functional materials. Recently, Cu-NPs deposited onto TiO2 nano-flowers has been reported for enhanced photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2O to CH3OH. Similarly, photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO over Cu-loaded TiO2 nanotubes arrays has been investigated. Besides, ZnFe2O4/TiO2 nano-belts have been inspected for CO2 reduction to fuels.

On the other hand, plasmonic photocatalysis has been reported as a capable system to improve efficiencies based on their localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect. More importantly, both Au and Ag have strong plasmonic effects which capable to improve semiconductor efficiency based on their LSPR effect. Loading plasmonic Au-NPs over TiO2 nanowires has been demonstrated as efficient surface modifiers to enhance TiO2 photoactivity for photocatalytic CO2 reduction via SPR effect of Au under visible light. Likewise, Au@TiO2 yolk shell hollow spheres for plasmon-induced photocatalytic reduction of CO2 to solar fuels has been investigated. Nevertheless, compared to Au, Ag is much cheaper, which can be used appropriately to enhance TiO2 photoactivity via LSPR effects photocatalytic CO2 system. In this case, strongly visible light responsive plasmonic AgX (X=Cl, Br) nanoparticles for photocatalytic reduction of CO2 to CH3OH has been reported. Liu et al. reported plasmonic Ag/TiO2 NRs for CO2 photoreduction using H2O reductant under visible light. The enhanced photoactivity of TiO2 NRs for CO2 reduction to CH3OH was evidently due to Ag-NPs SPR effect. Besides, insertion of metallic Ag-NPs onto semiconductor structure reduces the recombination rate of photo-generated charges (e−/h+) and improves photocatalytic activity. Moreover, size and shape of noble metals show different physical and chemical properties. When metals NPs of different sizes are loaded over the semiconductor surface, they perform different photocatalytic properties. Recently, size dependent effect of Au-loaded in g-C3N4/BiOBr/Au system for photocatalytic CO2 reduction has been reported. It was noticed that different sizes of Au-NPs have synergistic effects to enhance photoactivity under light irradiations. Therefore, it is vital to explore synergistic effects of Ag-NPs co-coated over TiO2 NWs for selective photocatalytic CO2 reduction because of its low cost and higher productivity.

In addition of efficient photocatalysts, the reductant choice is of great importance, as it effects the overall CO2 reduction process efficiency and products selectivity. In order to achieve the reduction of CO2, H2O is usually fed as a reducing agent. Thermodynamically, photocatalytic conversion of CO2 with H2O over heterogeneous photocatalysis is not a favorable process because reduction of H+, released from H2O, usually competes with CO2 reduction. This is because H2O reduction potential to genertae H2 is lower (0eV) than the CO2 standard reduction potential (-1.9eV). Under such conditions, a reduction competition can be developed between CO2/H2O, thus photoreactions would be more favourable for conversion of H2O to H2 instead of CO2 reduction. Recently, we investigated H2 as a potentially viable reductant for CO2 reduction to CO and CH4 over different type of photocatalysts. The performance of photocatalysts were significantly enhanced when H2 was employed as a reducing agent compared to H2O for selective CO production. Therefore, it is apropriate to investigate H2 as a reductants for photocatalytic CO2 to CO conversion over plasmonic metal/TiO2 NWs based catalyst. To the best of our knowledge, the application of plasmonic Ag-NPs-promoted TiO2 NWs for the conversion of CO2 to CO with H2 as a reducing agent under visible light irradiations have never been reported.

Herein, we envisaged that plasmonic silver nanoparticles (Ag-NPs) modified TiO2 nanowires core/shell hetero-junction could efficiently reduce CO2 to CO via reverse water gas shift reaction (RWGS) reaction under visible light irradiation. The Ag-NPs-modified TiO2 NWs with different sizes of Ag-NPs were synthesized using a facile hydrothermal and photoreduction method. The reaction products were compared to understand the role of Ag-NPs for LSPR effect. The synergistic effect of plasmonic photocatalyst was further investigated under UV and visible light of different intensity. The stability test of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs was analyzed in a continuous operation of photoreactor. The plasmonic reaction mechanism of Ag-NPs in conjunction with LSPR excitation and charge transport to understand the reaction pathway is described.

The TiO2 NWs were prepared via a facile synthesis route according to our previous work. Typically, 1g of TiO2 powder was suspended in 8M NaOH solution, stirred for 10min and then transferred into 50mL Teflon-lined autoclave. The solution was stirred continuously at 110°C for 2h using a stirred tank reactor and then cooled to room temperature. The solids obtained were washed with deionized water and 0.1M HCl several times to reach pH below 9. After being dried, the products were calcined at 500°C for 5h. Ag-NPs coated over TiO2 NWs were prepared by photo-deposition method and the amount of Ag-NPs in each sample was controlled by the concentration of AgNO3 solution. For the deposition of silver (Ag-NPs) on the TiO2 NWs, 0.50g of TiO2 powder was dispersed in 20mL of water and then a certain volume of 0.025M AgNO3 solution was added into it. The solution was photo-irradiated for 15min using 200W Hg lamp of light intensity 150mW/cm2 at wavelength 252nm to get gray precipitations. The precipitates obtained were filtered, dried and calcined at 500°C for 5h. The different volumes of AgNO3 solution were used to get Ag loading in TiO2 of 1, 2, 3 and 5wt.%, respectively. The pure TiO2 NWs were synthesized using the same procedure. The schematic illustrations for fabrication of Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs is depicted shown in Fig. 1 .

X-ray powder diffraction (XRD) was recorded on a Bruker D 8 advance diffractometer with Cu- Kα radiation (λ=1.54Å, operated at 40kV and 40mA) to identify the phase structures and phase transformation of all the samples. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was performed using JEOL-TEM apparatus operating with an acceleration voltage of 200kV, which was used to measure the particle sizes and d-spacing of the sample. The XPS spectra were calibrated with respect to the binding energy of the C1s signal at 284.60eV as the internal standard. Nitrogen-adsorption-desorption isotherms were collected using Micromeritics ASAP 2020 at 77K, after degassing the samples at 523K for 4h under vacuum and using the nitrogen flux. The Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area and pore diameters were calculated from the desorption branch of isotherms according to BJH method. Ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) diffuse reflectance absorbance spectra were carried out on a Cary 100 Agilent UV–vis spectrophotometer equipped with an integrated sphere in the wavelength range of 200–800nm. Raman and photoluminescence (PL) spectra of samples were recorded on a Raman Xplora Plus Spectrophotometer (HORIBA Scientific) with a 600nm grating and a 532nm emitting laser as an excitation source.

The photocatalytic reduction of CO2 with H2 was carried out in a photocatalytic reactor of volume 108cm3. A 35W car HID lamp was used as a visible light source with a light intensity 20mW/cm2 measured using a reference solar cell (91150V, Newport). The photoactivity was further investigated using a solar simulator LCS-100 (Newport) integrated with UV-cut filters with light intensity equal to one solar spectrum. Similarly, a 200W Hg reflector lamp with a light intensity of 150mW/cm2 was used as a source of UV-light irradiation. The UV-light intensity was measured using an online optical process monitor ILT OPM-1D and a SED008/W sensor. The lamps were located at the top of the reactor equipped with a quartz window of 10mm thickness for passing of light irradiations. Typically, 10mg powder photo-catalyst was dispersed uniformly at the bottom of the reactor and was purged using helium (He) as a carrier gas. Compressed CO2 and H2 (purity >99.99%) were regulated by mass flow controllers (MFC). The reactor pressure was maintained at 0.20bar above the atmospheric pressure for the batch mode experiment by closing the outlet valves. The gas feed ratio of CO2 and H2 of 1 was used for all the experiments. For CO2 reduction under continuous flow operation, gas mixture was continuously passed through the reactor at a total gas flow rate of 20mL/min. The operating conditions used were CO2/H2 feed ratio 1.0, temperature 100 ∘C and pressure 1atm.

The CO2 reduction products were analyzed using an online gas chromatograph (GC-Agilent Technologies 6890N, USA) equipped with FID and TCD detectors (GC/FID/TCD). FID detector was connected with a HP-PLOT Q capillary column (Agilent, length 30m. ID 0.53mm, film 40μm) for separation of C1–C4 paraffin and olefins hydrocarbons, alcohols and oxygenated compounds. The TCD detector was connected to UCW982, DC-200, Porapak Q and Mol Sieve 5A columns. Similarly, Porapak Q and DC-200 columns were used for separation of C1–C5 compounds while light gasses (H2, O2, N2, CO) were separated using MS-5A column.

Fig. 2 (a) shows XRD patterns of the pure TiO2 NWs and Ag-loaded TiO2 NWs with different Ag-contents. The TiO2 NWs with and without Ag-loading present similar patterns of peaks located at 2θ=25.31° (101), 2θ=37.80° (004), 2θ=48.0° (200), 2θ=53.87° (105), 2θ=55.08° (211), 2θ=62.73° (204), 2θ=68.75° (116), 2θ=70.25° (220), 2θ=75.09° (215). This illustrates pure anatase phase of TiO2 with growth axis in (101) directions. The diffraction peaks for Ag-NPs were not detected, which may result from the low-loading content or fine dispersion of Ag-NPs on the surface of TiO2 crystal. The patterns revealed that the photo-deposition of Ag-NPs did not affect the crystal structure of TiO2. Similar observations have been reported previously.

Fig. 2(b) depicts Raman spectra of the pure TiO2 and Ag-loaded TiO2 NWs samples. The characteristics bands of TiO2 NPs and TiO2 NWs samples have similar reflections, and the peaks are relatively sharp and stronger than the Ag-loaded TiO2 NWs samples. In pure TiO2, the intense Raman signals with Eg(1) mode appeared at 143cm−1 followed by low intense modes Eg(2) and Eg(3) located at 196cm−1 and 635cm−1, respectively. B1g peak appeared at 394cm−1 and (A1g +B1g) reflected as a single merged peak at 511cm−1. All these peaks reveal the characteristics of the pure anatase phase of TiO2. The Raman spectra of Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs samples are identical to that of the pure TiO2 NWs, which clearly indicated that the TiO2 retained its structure after incorporation of these metals. However, Ag NPs relating signals were not identified because of the relatively low concentrations and due to the weak Raman scattering of these metals. However, changes are obvious in the position and width of the Ag NPs modified TiO2 peaks. With the loading of Ag NPs, the Raman band Eg(1) is slightly shifted towards higher wavenumber, Raman band B1g and Eg(3) was broadened and their intensities were reduced. This indicated that the interaction between Ag-NPs and TiO2 NWs affected the Raman resonance of the TiO2. These observations have confirmed successful deposition of Ag-NPs over the TiO2 NWs surface without any phase change.

The morphology of Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs is examined using TEM as illustrated in Fig. 3 . Fig. 3(a–c) show uniform distribution of Ag-NPs over the surface of TiO2 NWs. The TiO2 NWs detected were of different size with diameter in the range of 20–50nm. The particle size distribution of Ag-NPs is depicted in Fig. 3(b), which revealed Ag-NPs are very fine, with diameter range of 1.3–14nm. Two mean diameters were detected with their values of∼2nm and∼8nm, respectively. The amounts of large size plasmonic Ag-NPs existing in the sample are approximately the same as the small size Ag-NPs. More importantly, the small size Ag-NPs presented over the TiO2 NWs surface can serve as electrons sink to promote the charges separation. Fig. 3(d) exhibits the crystal structure of the Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs hybrids measured using a high resolution TEM. The spacing between two adjacent lattice fringes to (101) plane of anatase TiO2 and (111) plane of Ag-NP were 0.35nm and 0.24nm, respectively.

The N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms of the pure TiO2, TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs modified TiO2 NWs samples are depicted in Fig. 4 . The isotherms of the pure TiO2, TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs are similar to type IV curve with the hysteresis loops which is the characteristics of mesoporous materials. The BET surface area, pore volume and pore diameter of the TiO2, TiO2 NWs and modified TiO2 NWs samples are summarized in Table 1 . BET specific surface area (SBET) of the pure TiO2 was 42 increased to 72m2 g−1 for TiO2 NWs. On the other hand, BET surface area gradually decreased to 48m2 g−1 when 3wt.% Ag-NPs was loaded to TiO2 NWs. This decreased in the BET surface area could be accounted for partial TiO2 NWs surface coverage by the deposited Ag-NPs. Similar observations were obtained in BJH adsorption pore volumes. In the case of pore diameter, pure TiO2 pore diameter was 10nm, increased to 25nm in TiO2 NWs, obviously due to the larger diameter of TiO2 NWs. A further increase in pore diameter was observed in Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs evidently due to deposited Ag-NPs layer over the surface of these materials.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) was used to analyze chemical states of the elements in Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs as shown in Fig. 5 . Fig. 5(a) reveals the presence of Ti2p peaks namely Ti2p3/2 and Ti2p1/2 located at 458.06eV and 363.79eV, respectively, corresponds to Ti4+ oxidation state or titanium dioxide (TiO2). The Ag3d spectrum with BE regions centered at 367. 55eV (3d5/2) and 373.53eV (3d3/2), indicating the presence of silver in metal state as depicted in Fig. 5(b). Fig. 5(c) shows the O1s spectrum with main components, one at 530.87eV, ascribed to the lattice oxygen O2 and binding energy component located at 532.98eV related to metal-OH bonds or free hydroxyl group (OH) on the surface. The spectrum of C 1s with peaks located at 284.60eV and 288.44eV are presented in Fig. 5(d). The main peak at 284.60eV is assigned to CC and CH hydrocarbon bonds. The peak at 288.44eV can be attributed to carbon atoms bound to oxygen with double bond CO. The relative concentration of peak at 284.60eV was much more and may be recognized as the carbon from carbon tap used for sample analysis.

UV–vis diffuse reflectance absorbance spectra of TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs modified TiO2 NWs are shown in Fig. 6 . Fig. 6(a) shows the UV–vis diffuse reflectance absorbance spectra of TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs modified TiO2 NWs. Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs shows a broad visible light absorption due to LSPR absorption of Ag-NPs, indicating metallic Ag exists as recognized by XPS and TEM analysis. More importantly, LSPR images could be seen in Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs samples, when excited with a laser light of wavelength 532nm, as depicted in the inset of Fig. 6(b). The band gap energy was calculated according to plot of (αhv)2 vs. photon energy as depicted in Fig. 6(c). The band gap energy of 3.10, 3.17 and 3.16eV was obtained for TiO2, TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs, respectively. The TiO2 band gap energy has increased perhaps due to the pure anatase phase and larger crystallite size of TiO2 NWs compared to TiO2 nanoparticles. Ag-NPs have no significant influence on increasing the band gap energy of TiO2 NWs. However, enhanced visible light absorption evidenced due to a broadband peak located at around 580nm arising from SPR of Ag-NPs in the TiO2 matrix.

Fig. 7 shows PL emission spectra of the pure TiO2 NWs and Ag-NPs modified TiO2 NWs samples excited at a wavelength of 532nm. The broad symmetric peaks appeared at 536nm revealed that emission is not because of TiO2 band edge excitation. Therefore, PL signals can be attributed to the transition of electrons from the oxygen vacancies to TiO2 valance band. It is noticeable that emission spectra of the Ag-modified TiO2 samples are similar to those of the pure TiO2 NWs sample. However, the PL intensity enfeebled in Ag-NPs sample. The electron transfers from the TiO2 NWs to Ag-promoted TiO2 NWs are more efficient, resulting in hindered charges recombination rate.

The control experiments for photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2 were conducted at 100°C for 2h under visible light irradiation. Using all types of catalysts, carbon containing compounds were not detected in the reaction system without reactants or light irradiations. The effects of Ag-NPs on TiO2 NWs performance for CO2 photoreduction with H2 to CO is shown in Fig. 8 (a). Pure TiO2 has low photoactivity for CO production, which gradually increased using TiO2 NWs. This was perhaps due to efficient charges transfer and higher surface area in TiO2 NWs. Loading Ag-NPs into TiO2 NWs significantly improved CO2 photoreduction with optimum Ag-NPs contents of 3wt.%. However, with higher Ag-loading (e.g. 5wt.%) photoactivity was reduced, possibly Ag-NPs were adjacent to each other over TiO2 NWs, electron-hole charges recombine immediately, resulting in lower photoactivity. The significantly enhanced photoactivity of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs samples were evidently due to plasmonic effect with efficient charges separation by Ag-NPs.

The performance of Ag-NP on the photoactivity of TiO2 NWs for photocatalytic CO2 conversion with H2 to CH4 and CH3OH is presented in Fig. 8(b). Using pure TiO2 NWs, only small amount of CH4 was produced which was considerably enhanced in Ag-NPs loading TiO2 NWs samples. The maximum yield of CH4 was detected at optimum Ag-NPs-loading of 3wt.% and then gradually declined. On the other hand, CH3OH production was not detected in the pure TiO2 but its production was evidenced in all the Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs samples. The Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs exhibits higher photoactivity for CO2 reduction, where the yield of CH3OH was increased gradually by increasing the contents of Ag-NPs. The optimal 3wt.% Ag-loading was observed and its production trends were similar to that of CH4 production. These observations have confirmed that plasmon-excited electron can be injected into TiO2 for its excitation. On the other hand, an instant charge separation can be achieved on the Ag-NPs due to synergistic effect resulting in prolonged recombination time of the photo-generated charges. In this way, enhanced photoactivity could be achieved for visible light driven reduction of CO2 to CO, CH4 and CH3OH.

The yield rates of different products are presented in Table 2 . The yield of CO over Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs was 983μmole g-catal.−1 h−1, a 23 times more than TiO2 NWs and 109 times higher than TiO2. It is likely to see that 13μmole g-catal.−1 h−1 of CH3OH was produced over Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs but was not detected in TiO2 and TiO2 NWs. These revealed Ag-NPs are also favorable for CH3OH production. The selectivity of CO production over Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs increased to 98%, confirming selective CO2 reduction using H2 as a reducing agent. The CO2 and H2 conversions over Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs were 1.43% and 2.35%, respectively. It is remarkable to see that the conversion of H2 was higher in Ag-loaded TiO2 NWs samples. According to the stoichiometric reaction in Eq. (1), one mole of H2 is required to produce one mole of CO. (1) CO 2 + H 2 → A g / T i O 2 N W s CO + H 2 O

As the selectivity of CO is near to 98%, suggesting CO2 and H2 consumption would be approximately much closer. Conversely, the higher H2 conversion during CO2 photo-reduction with H2 over plasmonic Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs was certainly due to some amount of hydrogen consumed by the silver during its oxidation/reduction process under light irradiations. Therefore, enhanced photoactivity of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs was mainly governed by the visible light absorption, higher surface area, photo-generated charges separation and SPR effect of Ag-NPs.

In order to investigate the performance of selective CO2 photoreduction to CO by H2 reducing agent over core-shell Ag NPs/TiO2 NWs photocatalysts under visible light irradiations, the results are compared with the work reported by various researchers. Kong et al. reported CO2 reduction with H2O over Ag/TiO2 nanorods with CH4 yield of 2.64μmoleg.catal−1 h−1, a 5 fold higher than TiO2 nanorods. CO2 reduction with H2O to CO was reported over g-C3N4-N-TiO2 in batch mode operation with a maximum yield 14.73μmole after 12h irradiation time. Over I/TiO2 and Cu-I/TiO2, a CO yield rate of 3.9 and 12μmole g-catal.−1 was reported after 3.5h during gas phase CO2 reduction in a batch mode operation. However, in current study, CO2 reduction with H2 to CO at selectivity 98% significantly enhanced using Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs core/shell hetero-junction. A comparison study between previous reports and current study revealed significantly improved photoactivity and selectivity using Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs photocatalysts.

The efficiency of Ag-NPs modified TiO2 NWs was further examined based on the quantum yield, calculated for each experiment, as the ratio of the product rate (mole per sec) with photonic flux (mole per sec). The quantum yield of CO2 photoreduction can be defined as the ratio of amount of products (mole per sec) with photonic flux (mole per sec) as shown in Eq. (2). (2) Quantum yield ( % ) = n × production rate ( mol/sec ) moles of photon flux ( mol/sec ) × 100

The quantum yield was calculated based on 2, 6 and 8 electrons (n) used for CO, CH3OH and CH4 production rate and moles of photon input energy over the catalyst surface. The quantum yields (QY) of CO, CH3OH and CH4 production over 3wt.% Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs were 0.15%, 0.01% and 0.006%, respectively (Table 1). The significantly enhanced QY over Ag-NPs/TiO2 was evidently due to efficient charge transfer rate and SPR effect of Ag-NPs.

It is generally accepted that the photocatalyst efficiency is mainly dependent on the light absorption ability, surface properties (e.g., specific surface area, pore structure, pore volume and adsorption property etc.) and photo-generated electron/hole pairs separation efficiency. It is evidenced that photoactivity for CO evolution rate over the TiO2 NWs can be improved by 23 fold via 3wt.% Ag-NPs loading. However, as discussed above that the TiO2 NWs surface area is much higher than the Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs, indicating that this factor is not crucial to the photocatalytic activity for Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs. Therefore, the enhanced photocatalytic activity of core/shell Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs hetero-junction can be mainly attributed to LSPR excitation of TiO2 NWs under visible light and charges separation by Ag-NPs. This synergistic effect between Ag-NPs and TiO2 NWs can greatly promote the production and separation of photo-generated carriers under visible light irradiation

The effects of UV and visible light irradiations on the photoactivity of Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs catalyst were investigated in a continuous photoreactor, since the catalyst active sites were utilized more for CO2 reduction over the irradiation time than the batch process. Besides, commercially continuous processes are preferable for fuel production. Fig. 9 (a) depicts the continuous production of CO over Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs under UV-light and visible-light irradiation at different reaction times. Evidently, different amounts of CO were produced during photo-induced CO2-hydrogen reactions under UV-light and visible-light of different intensities. The UV-light irradiation can produce more electron-hole pairs over the TiO2 surface due to short wavelength and higher photon energy (150mW/cm2). Therefore, the production of CO as the main product was found to be higher using UV-light irradiation. However, the deactivation of catalyst was found after 60min, after which CO yield dropped rapidly. On the other hand, using visible light irradiations, Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs photocatalyst found to be efficient for continuous production of CO over the entire irradiation time. The simulated sunlight contains the same spectra as the real sunlight with intensity 100mW/cm2, while the visible lamp (Car-HID lamp) has the light intensity of 20mW/cm2. Therefore, the amount of CO produced was different due to different in light intensities. Using solar simulator the yield of CO produced was 3.17 fold more than using visible-light (Car-HID lamp). Therefore, the plasmonic effect of Ag-NPs-promoted the photoactivity of TiO2 NWs under visible light irradiations.

The photocatalytic CO2 reduction to CH4 under visible and UV-light is depicted in Fig. 9(b). The production of CH4 was significant using solar simulated light which revealed that visible light is encouraging for the production of useful chemicals. The decreased in CH4 production over the irradiation time was probably, initially, some amount of CO was converted to CH4, when there was more production of electrons at the start of the reaction. In general, significantly enhanced photoactivity of Ag-NPs loaded over TiO2 NWs toward CO2 reduction was evidently due to synergistic effects of Ag-NPs for the absorption of visible light and efficient separation of charges over the TiO2 NWs surface.

The stability of Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs catalyst was further investigated to evaluate the life of catalyst under UV and visible light irradiations. In order to investigate the stability of Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs catalyst, all the experiments were repeated in cyclic runs under the identical conditions. The stability test for photocatalytic CO2 reduction with H2 to CO for Ag-NPs-loaded TiO2 NWs catalyst is presented in Fig. 10 (a). After each cycle, the reactor was purged with helium for one hour before starting the next run. Noticeably, the CO yield was decreased gradually over the irradiation time in cyclic runs under UV-light irradiation. However, photoactivity of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs was very stable under visible light irradiation (20mW/cm2). This has confirmed prolonged photoactivity of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs for continuous CO production under visible light. Recently, Qi et al. reported a gradual decrease in photoactivity of Ag-AgCl/TiO2 NWs for methyl orange degradation. However, the extended stability of Ag-NPs/TiO2 in the current study was apparently due to gas-solid heterogeneous system under low energy irradiation.

The stability analysis of Ag-NPs loaded TiO2 NWs for CH4 production in each cyclic run is illustrated in Fig. 10(b). Compared to the first cyclic run, in the second cyclic run, the CH4 production increased significantly at the start of the run and then gradually decreased. The higher CH4 production could be attributed to conversion of carbon with hydrogen deposited over the catalyst surface to CH4. However, in third cyclic run, CH4 yield increased and then decreased over the irradiation time. Seemingly, the intermediate species deposited over the catalyst surface could have been converted to CH4. However, Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs catalyst found to be very stable for continuous production of CH4 in cyclic runs.

The reaction mechanism of CO2 reduction over semiconductor photocatalyst involves multiple stages during which electrons and protons are transferred. Generally, the production and separation of charges over the photocatalysts is ascribed to the types of light irradiation, band gap energy of semiconductor and characteristics of metals used for doping of semiconductors. The visible light can provide an energy transfer channel while the light captured by TiO2 NWs can be reused by Ag-NPs resulting in enhanced LSPR effect. The schematic representation of surface plasmon resonance effect and photo-generated charge transfer process in Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs catalyst under UV and visible light irradiation is illustrated in Fig. 11 and Eqs. (3)–(10). Upon UV irradiation to photocatalyst, electron-hole pairs are induced in TiO2 photocatalyst. The photo-generated electrons, have high affinity to be trapped by Ag. In later stages, electrons are supposedly captured by CO2 in the present of cationic H2, results in the reduction of CO2 to CO. Under visible light, due to localized SPR of Ag-NPs, incident visible light induced the electric field in large size Ag-NPs and electrons could have been injected to TiO2 CB for its excitation. Simultaneously, electrons could be captured by small size Ag-NPs, thus an effective charge separation can be achieved. This size dependent effect of Ag-NPs has significant contribution in production and separation of charges under visible light irradiations. This resulted in enhanced TiO2 NWs photoactivity towards CO2 reduction to CO under visible light irradiation. The electrons on Ag-NPs are then injected to CO2 for its reduction while holes are consumed for H2 oxidation. The produced hydrogen radicals together with the electrons reduced CO2 to CO, CH3OH and CH4. The production of CO as the main product was due to reverse water gas shift reaction and evidently due to difference in kinetic rates for CO2 reduction products. Therefore, the enhanced photocatalytic activity of Ag-NPs-promoted TiO2 NWs core-shell hetero-junction can be attributed to synergistic effect of Ag-NPs toward efficient visible-light absorption and electron sinks for selective photo-induced CO2-to-CO conversion.

The Ag-NPs deposited TiO2 NWs core-shell hetero-junction was successfully investigated for selective CO2 photoreduction to CO under UV and visible light irradiations. The photocatalytic CO evolution rates were significantly enhanced in the presence of Ag-NPs as a shell on TiO2 NWs. The CO production rate is up to 983μmole g-catal.−1 h−1 at selectivity 98% and apparent quantum yield of 0.15%. The other products detected in adequate amounts were CH4 and CH3OH. Stability test confirmed prolonged stability of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs for selective CO production under visible light irradiations. The improved photocatalytic activity of Ag-NPs/TiO2 NWs is ascribed to the synergic effect, charger transfer property and the SPR effect of Ag-NPs.
